title: Classic Lined Tote Bag
summary: A sturdy canvas tote with a boxed base, cotton lining and an inside pocket.
description: This is the perfect first 'real' project: straight seams, a clean lined finish, and techniques you'll use again and again — boxed corners, strap making and topstitching. The canvas outer stands up on its own, and the size is fully adjustable before you cut.

params.label: Finished width
params.help: Across the front of the bag.

params.label: Base depth
params.help: Width of the flat base (boxed corners).

params.label: Handle length
params.help: Visible handle length. 60 cm sits on the shoulder; 44 cm is hand-held.

customNote: Width, height, depth and handle length use this pattern's own rules: body pieces grow by the finished size plus the base depth and seam allowances; boxed-corner squares are always half the depth; strap width and the pocket stay fixed. Nothing is scaled proportionally.

tools.name: Sewing machine
tools.why: All seams are machine-sewn for strength.

tools.name: Universal or denim needle 90/14
tools.why: Canvas is thick — finer needles bend or skip stitches.

tools.name: Fabric scissors
tools.why: Clean cuts through two layers of canvas.

tools.name: Quilting ruler or long straight ruler
Pins or sewing clips
tools.why: Holding layers. Clips are easier on thick canvas.

tools.name: Iron & ironing board
tools.why: Pressing folds and seams is half the work.

tools.name: Hand-sewing needle
tools.why: Only if you close the lining gap by hand.

materials.name: Main fabric — cotton canvas
materials.why: Forms the outside and the handles; needs body so the bag stands up.

materials.name: Lining — quilting cotton
alternatives: An old cotton shirt or pillowcase
materials.why: Hides the seams and makes the bag tidy inside. Also used for the pocket.

materials.name: All-purpose polyester thread
materials.why: Polyester is stronger than cotton thread for bags.
alternatives: Topstitching thread for the final topstitch

pieces.name: Outer body
markings: Cut a {D/2} square from both bottom corners

pieces.name: Handle
pieces.notes: Folded strap — no seam allowance on the long edges. Length includes {ins} at each end that is caught in the top seam.

pieces.name: Pocket
pieces.notes: Folded in half at the top so the pocket opening is a clean fold.

steps.title: Pre-wash and press your fabric
steps.text: Wash and dry both fabrics the way you'll wash the finished bag, then press out every crease. Canvas often shrinks 3–5% on its first wash.
steps.beginner: If you skip this, the canvas may shrink later while the lining doesn't — the lining then bags out or the outer puckers. Press with steam on the cotton setting, lifting and lowering the iron.
tips: Zig-zag the cut ends before washing so they don't unravel into a tangle.
warnings: Irons are hot: keep the cord clear and stand it upright when not in use.
steps.alt: The canvas and lining fabrics laid flat with an iron pressing them after washing.

steps.title: Set up your machine for canvas
steps.text: Fit a 90/14 universal or denim needle and wind a bobbin. Set a straight stitch of 3 mm. Sew a test seam through two layers of canvas scrap and check that the stitches look the same on both sides.
steps.beginner: If loops appear underneath, re-thread the top thread with the presser foot UP. If the top thread looks tight and pulls the bobbin thread up, lower the top tension by one number.
steps.expert: 90/14 needle, 3 mm straight stitch, test on two layers.
warnings: Keep fingers clear of the needle. Switch the machine off when changing needles or feet.
steps.alt: A test seam on two layers of canvas scrap under the presser foot, with stitch length 3 millimetres marked.

steps.title: Cut the outer body and handles
steps.text: Fold the canvas lengthwise, right sides together, so the selvedges meet. Using the cutting layout, measure and mark the outer body rectangle and one handle strip, keeping the long sides parallel to the selvedge. Cut through both layers so you get two of each.
steps.beginner: The grainline arrow on each piece must run parallel to the selvedge (the firm finished edge). Measure from the fold to each corner rather than eyeballing it, and double-check every measurement before cutting.
steps.expert: Cut 2 body + 2 handles from folded canvas per layout.
tips: Mark with chalk on the wrong side.
Check the rectangle is square: both diagonals should measure the same.
warnings: Cut away from your body; with a rotary cutter, close the blade every time you put it down.
steps.alt: Cutting layout for the canvas showing two stacked layers with the body rectangle and handle strip placed along the grain.

steps.title: Cut the lining and pocket
steps.text: Fold the lining fabric the same way and cut two lining body pieces. Then cut ONE pocket through a single layer. Mark a 12 cm turning gap centred on the bottom edge of one lining piece.
steps.beginner: For the single pocket, fold the top layer of fabric back out of the way, or cut from an unfolded area, so you don't cut two.
steps.expert: Cut 2 lining + 1 pocket; mark 12 cm gap on one lining base.
steps.alt: Cutting layout for the lining fabric with two lining bodies cut on the double and one pocket cut through a single layer.

steps.title: Cut the boxed-corner squares
steps.text: On all four body pieces (2 outer, 2 lining), mark a square at both bottom corners measured from the raw edges, then cut the squares away. Label each piece with chalk (OUTER / LINING).
steps.beginner: These squares are what give the bag its flat base. Their size is always half the base depth. Measure from the cut edges, not from where the seam will be.
steps.expert: Remove D/2 squares from both bottom corners of all 4 body pieces.
steps.alt: A body panel with a small square removed from each bottom corner, each side of the square labelled half the base depth.

steps.title: Press the handles into four layers
steps.text: Take one handle strip. Press it in half lengthwise, wrong sides together, and open it out. Fold both long raw edges in to meet the centre crease and press. Fold in half again along the original crease and press firmly. Repeat for the second handle.
steps.beginner: You end up with a strip four layers thick with all raw edges hidden inside — no turning needed. Steam and a firm press make the next step much easier.
steps.expert: Press handles to 4-fold, finished width shown.
warnings: Keep fingertips clear of the iron when pressing narrow folds — use a seam gauge or wooden tool to hold the fold.

els.text: 2 · fold edges to the centre crease

steps.alt: Three stages of a handle strip: pressed in half, raw edges folded to the centre, then folded again into a narrow four-layer strap.

steps.title: Edgestitch both handles
steps.text: Edgestitch along both long edges of each handle, 3 mm from the edge, starting with the open side. Sew slowly and keep the folds aligned.
steps.beginner: Stitching the open edge first locks all four layers before they can shift. Stitching the folded edge as well makes the handles symmetrical and stronger.
steps.expert: Edgestitch both long edges at 3 mm.

els.text: open edge first, then folded edge

steps.alt: A handle strap with stitching 3 millimetres from both long edges, the presser foot sewing the top edge.

steps.title: Sew the pocket
steps.text: Fold the pocket in half, right sides together, so the fold is at the top. Sew the two sides and the bottom with a 1 cm seam, leaving a 6 cm gap in the bottom. Backstitch at both sides of the gap. Clip the corners, turn right side out, push out the corners and press, tucking the gap's seam allowances inside.
steps.beginner: The fold becomes the pocket's top edge, so it's clean without hemming. The gap gets closed automatically when you sew the pocket onto the lining.
steps.expert: Fold RST, sew 3 sides at 1 cm with 6 cm gap, clip, turn, press.
steps.alt: The pocket folded in half with stitching down both sides and along the bottom, a gap left in the middle of the bottom seam.

steps.title: Attach the pocket to the lining
steps.text: Place the lining piece WITHOUT the turning gap right side up. Centre the pocket on it with the pocket's folded edge 8 cm below the lining's top edge. Pin, then edgestitch down one side, across the bottom (closing the gap) and up the other side. Reinforce each top corner with a small triangle of stitching.
steps.beginner: Measure from both side edges to make sure it's centred. The triangles at the top corners take the strain when you push things into the pocket.
steps.expert: Centre pocket 8 cm below lining top; edgestitch 3 sides, bartack top corners.
steps.alt: The pocket centred on a lining panel 8 centimetres below the top, stitched on three sides with small triangles at the top corners.

steps.title: Sew the outer bag
steps.text: Place the two outer body pieces right sides together and clip. Sew down one side, across the bottom and up the other side with a 1 cm seam, backstitching at each end. Leave the cut-out corner squares unsewn. Press the seams open.
steps.beginner: Your stitching should stop exactly where the cut-out begins on each corner — don't sew around the notch. Pressing seams open now makes the boxed corners line up neatly.
steps.expert: Outer RST; sew sides + base at 1 cm, leave corners open; press open.
steps.alt: Two outer panels right sides together, stitched along both sides and the bottom, with the corner notches left unsewn.

steps.title: Box the outer corners
steps.text: At one corner, pull the front and back apart and flatten the opening so the side seam sits directly on top of the bottom seam, forming a straight edge. Nest the pressed-open seams, clip, and sew straight across with a 1 cm seam. Backstitch twice — this seam takes the weight of the bag. Repeat on the other corner.
steps.beginner: Feel through the fabric with your fingers that the two seams line up exactly. If they don't, the base will twist.
steps.expert: Box corners: match seams, sew across at 1 cm, double backstitch.
steps.alt: A bag corner pinched into a triangle with the seams aligned and a straight seam sewn across, the length of which equals the base depth.

steps.title: Sew and box the lining
steps.text: Repeat steps 10 and 11 with the two lining pieces, right sides together — but leave the 12 cm turning gap in the bottom seam open, backstitching on both sides of it. Box both lining corners.
steps.beginner: The gap must be in a straight part of the bottom seam, not near a corner. Backstitch firmly on each side because you'll pull the whole bag through it.
steps.expert: Lining as outer, leaving 12 cm gap in base.
steps.alt: Lining panels sewn on the sides and bottom with a 12 centimetre gap left open in the middle of the bottom seam.

steps.title: Baste the handles to the outer bag
steps.text: Turn the outer bag right side out. On the front, place the ends of one handle with their raw ends level with the top edge and the loop hanging down over the bag. Position each end so its outer edge is the distance shown from the side seam. Check the handle isn't twisted, then baste 5 mm from the top edge. Repeat on the back, matching the position exactly.
steps.beginner: Basting means a long, temporary stitch — it just holds the handle while you sew the real seam. The handles hang downwards now and flip up when the bag is turned.
steps.expert: Baste handle ends at top edge, outer edges at W/4 from side seams; check no twist.

measurements.label: Handle outer edge from side seam

steps.alt: A handle with both ends basted at the top edge of the outer bag, loop hanging down, each end positioned a quarter of the bag width from the side.

steps.title: Join outer and lining at the top
steps.text: Leave the lining wrong side out. Slide the outer bag (right side out, handles hanging inside) into the lining so their right sides face. Match the side seams, nest them in opposite directions, and clip all around the top edge. Sew around the top with a 1 cm seam.
steps.beginner: It looks strange: you'll see the wrong side of the lining on the outside and nothing of the canvas except the top edge. That's correct. Sew slowly over the handles — there are lots of layers there.
steps.expert: Outer into lining RST, match side seams, sew top at 1 cm.
tips: Use a free-arm if your machine has one.
Hand-walk the needle over the handle layers.
steps.alt: The outer bag nested inside the inside-out lining, clipped around the top edge with a seam one centimetre down.

args.label: turn right side out through the lining gap

steps.title: Turn the bag right side out
steps.text: Reach into the turning gap in the lining and gently pull the outer bag through it. Then push the lining down inside the outer bag. Use a point turner to push out the boxed corners.
steps.beginner: Go slowly — pull from the base of the bag, not the handles. It will look crumpled; pressing fixes that.
steps.expert: Turn through the gap; push lining inside.
steps.alt: The bag being pulled right side out through the gap in the lining.

steps.title: Close the turning gap
steps.text: Pull the lining out of the bag. Tuck the gap's seam allowances inside so the folds line up with the seam, and edgestitch the gap closed by machine, or ladder-stitch it by hand for an invisible finish. Push the lining back inside.
steps.beginner: Machine-sewing it shut is perfectly fine — it ends up at the bottom of the bag where nobody sees it.
steps.alt: Close-up of the tucked-in edges of the turning gap stitched shut close to the fold.

steps.title: Press and topstitch the top edge
steps.text: Roll the seam at the top edge so it sits exactly on the edge, and press all the way around. Topstitch 5 mm from the top edge, through the outer, lining and handles, with a 3–3.5 mm stitch. Start and end at a side seam.
steps.beginner: Topstitching keeps the lining from creeping out and adds strength where the handles are. Use the side of the presser foot as a guide.
steps.expert: Press top edge; topstitch 5 mm, 3.5 mm stitch.
warnings: Steam is hot — keep your hand outside the bag when pressing the top edge.
steps.alt: The top edge of the bag pressed and topstitched 5 millimetres from the edge, crossing the handles.

steps.title: Final press and check
steps.text: Give the whole bag a final press. Check: both handles are the same length and not twisted, the boxed corners are symmetric, no lining shows at the top, and all thread ends are trimmed.
steps.beginner: Pull firmly on each handle to test it before you load the bag up. If any stitch looks loose, sew over it again.
steps.expert: Final press, QC handles and corners, trim threads.
steps.alt: The finished tote bag with circles highlighting the handle joins and the base corners to check.

review.note: Dimensions follow standard lined-tote construction and are internally consistent, but this sample has not yet been test-sewn.
